analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 2-3% annual tax on wealth above $50 million.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would place a yearly tax on the net worth of roughly the wealthiest households in America: 2% on wealth between $50 million and $1 billion, and 3% above $1 billion (rising to 6% if a national single-payer health program passed). People with less than $50 million in net worth would pay nothing. The bill also funds the IRS to enforce the tax and requires the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax filers each year.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with net worth under $50 million pay nothing, and the revenue would come only from the roughly 100,000 wealthiest households, much of whose wealth currently goes untaxed until assets are sold. The general public benefits if the revenue is used for public programs, though the bill does not itself direct the money to any specific use.

how_it_helps.text: The tax applies only to net worth above $50 million, so married couples below that threshold owe nothing under the bill [S3].
It taxes all property, real or personal, tangible or intangible, minus debts, closing in on forms of wealth that largely escape income tax until sold [S2][S3].
It requires the IRS to audit at least 30% of wealth-tax taxpayers annually and provides IRS funding for enforcement, taxpayer services, and systems modernization through FY2032 [S2][S3].
It penalizes large valuation understatements and curbs avoidance through foreign corporations, partnerships, and trusts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The roughly one-tenth of one percent of households with more than $50 million in net worth, including owners of large private businesses whose companies would have to be valued under new Treasury rules. Some of the tax could be passed to workers or consumers if business owners adjust, and critics warn some wealthy filers would move assets or renounce citizenship despite the bill's 40% exit tax on covered expatriates.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not earmark its revenue for any specific program; unless Congress later spends it, the money could simply offset deficits [S3].

Valuing hard-to-price assets like stakes in private companies is difficult and contested; the bill requires Treasury to create new formulaic valuation methods, which would face years of legal and administrative challenge [S3].
A direct tax on wealth has not previously been imposed under federal law; critics question whether it could survive a constitutional challenge, a dispute the bill text does not resolve [S3].

Rich families with strong tax planning could shift assets abroad or take other steps to minimize the tax, although the bill imposes a 40% tax on covered expatriates the day before expatriation to deter this [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would impose a modest annual levy on households that currently realize much of their gain untaxed, with most of the compliance burden falling on a very small group. Its main real-world weaknesses are administrative: valuing private businesses and trusts is hard, court challenges are likely, and avoidance planning would reduce collections. It is a large structural change whose benefits depend on later decisions about how the revenue is spent.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 2021 and stayed there until the two-year Congress ended, never coming up for a vote in the committee or on the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the Ultra-Millionaire Tax Act of 2021 on March 1, 2021, with 32 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S5].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a markup or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with more than $50 million in net worth, whose wealth remains untaxed annually, along with the private-asset valuation status quo; the bill's supporters gained nothing from the outcome.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ultrawealthy households and asset-valuation status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote that would have tested whether any Republicans supported it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would tax their accumulated wealth annually, a cost that under current law largely arrives only when assets are sold or passed to heirs. The bill's death without a vote leaves current treatment in place.

Their companies would have to be valued under new Treasury formulaic methods each year, and payment could be deferred at most five years for liquidity-constrained owners. The bill never advanced, so no valuations were required.

industries.industry: Wealth management and trust services for the very wealthy
industries.note: The tax would have created new valuation, reporting, and avoidance-planning work even as it cut the wealth such firms manage. Nothing changed because the bill died.
